## Step 2 : Create the repo and the project

[!Phase 1: Environment|blue]

Before writing any code, create the project and put it under Git and GitHub. There are two routes: build every file by hand (Route A) or let `uv init` generate the base (Route B). Pick one. Both end with the same **my-project** structure and the same first commit on GitHub.

What you will do
Create a GitHub repo with the right settings, clone it locally, run uv init inside the cloned folder, then make your first commit and push.
----
::: steps
- Tell Git who you are (once per machine)
- Create the my-project folder and connect it to a GitHub repo
- Pin Python 3.12, create the virtual environment and pyproject.toml
- Create src/ and the support files
- Make the first commit and push
:::

::: info Why
Starting from Git and GitHub means every change is tracked from the first file. A fixed scaffold (pinned Python, one pyproject.toml, a lockfile, a clean .gitignore) gives everyone the same reproducible starting point.
:::

::: info Prerequisites
- Step 1 done: `uv --version` works
- Git installed, and a GitHub account
- Python 3.12 available (check with `python3 --version`)
:::
### 2.1 Create repo on GitHub 

Check your git locally as you tell Git who you are (once per machine) Without this, your first commit fails with "**Author identity unknown**". Use the same email as your GitHub account.

```bash title="Set and check your Git identity"
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```
→ The first two lines set the values.

```bash title="Set and check your Git identity"
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email

# fetch and push URLs:
# git remote -v
```
→ The first two lines print the values you set. last line shows fetch and push URLs.

Create Github repository locally
```bash title="Step A — Create repo on GitHub"
# Go to github.com → click "New repository"
#
# Naming conventions (important):
#   my-project            ← kebab-case, all lowercase
#   rag-learning-env      ← descriptive, short
#   NOT: MyProject  my_project  RAGProject
#
# Settings to fill in:
#   Repository name → your-repo-name
#   Description     → Production RAG learning environment
#   Visibility      → Public or Private
#   ✓ Add a README file
#   ✓ .gitignore template → Python
#   ✓ License → MIT
#
# Click "Create repository"
```

→ Or create a new repository on the command line
```bash title="Step A — Create repo on CLI"
echo "# RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD" >> README.md
git init
git add README.md
git commit -m "first commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/TheUniverseOfAI/RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD.git
git push -u origin main
```
→ Or push an existing repository from the command line
```bash title="Step A — Create repo on CLI"
git remote add origin https://github.com/TheUniverseOfAI/RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```
→ Do this on github.com before touching your terminal

```bash title="Step B — Clone the repo locally"
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPO_NAME.git
cd YOUR_REPO_NAME
```
→ Replace with your actual GitHub username and repo name

::: tip --global means once per machine
If you set this before, skip it. It applies to every repo on this machine.
:::

| Setup | Scope | Again for a new project? |
|---|---|---|
| git config --global user.name/email | Once per machine | No |
| git init | Once per project | Yes |
| Creating the GitHub repo | Once per project | Yes |
| git remote add origin | Once per project | Yes |
### 2.2 Choose your route

| | Route A: by hand | Route B: uv init |
|---|---|---|
| Start | Local folder first, then an **empty** GitHub repo | GitHub repo first (with README, .gitignore, license), then clone |
| Scaffold | You create each file yourself | `uv init .` generates the base, you adjust it |
| Best for | Learning what every file does | Speed, and starting from GitHub |
| End result | Same structure (see 2.4) | Same structure (see 2.4) |

::: important Pick one route
Do Route A **or** Route B, not both. Then continue at 2.4.
:::

### 2.3A Route A: build the project by hand

**A1. Create the project folder**

```bash title="Create and enter the folder"
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
```

→ Every command from now on runs from inside my-project/. Check with `pwd`.

**A2. Initialise Git locally**

```bash title="Initialise Git"
git init
git branch -M main
```

→ Creates the hidden .git/ folder and names the default branch main.

**A3. Create an empty repo on GitHub** Go to github.com, click **+**, then **New repository**. this step done above.

**A4. Connect the local repo to GitHub**. You can skip this feature you already connect your local to remote repo from steps above

```bash title="Remove any old origin, add the new one, confirm"
git remote remove origin 2>/dev/null
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/my-project.git
git remote -v
```

→ The first line is safe even if no origin exists. `git remote -v` shows your URL twice (fetch and push).

::: tip Why remove before adding?
`git remote add` fails with "remote origin already exists" if one is set. Remove first, and the pair never fails, however many times you run it.
:::

**A5. Create .gitignore**

```bash title="Create .gitignore"
touch .gitignore
```

Open .gitignore and paste:

```text title=".gitignore"
.venv/
.env
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
.DS_Store
*.egg-info/
dist/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
```

::: warning Never commit .venv/ or .env
The venv is large and machine-specific. .env holds your secret keys. Do not ignore .python-version: it must be committed.
:::

**A6. Pin Python 3.12 and create the virtual environment**

```bash title="Pin Python and create .venv"
uv python pin 3.12
uv venv
```

→ Creates .python-version and the .venv/ folder.

::: tabs
```bash title="Activate (macOS / Linux)"
source .venv/bin/activate
```
```powershell title="Activate (PowerShell)"
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```
```bash title="Activate (Git Bash)"
source .venv/Scripts/activate
```
:::

→ `(.venv)` appears at the start of your prompt. Optional: `uv run <command>` works without activating.

**A7. Create pyproject.toml**

```bash title="Create the file"
touch pyproject.toml
```

Open pyproject.toml and paste:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
name            = "my-project"
version         = "0.1.0"
description     = "Production RAG system"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies    = []

# build backend: Hatchling packages this teaching project
[build-system]
requires      = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

# this teaching project uses src itself as the import package
[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src"]

# ruff: linter
[tool.ruff]
line-length    = 100
target-version = "py312"

# pytest: test runner
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

→ Dependencies stay empty on purpose. Packages are added later, one at a time.

::: warning Why Hatchling
An older setuptools backend fails with "No module named setuptools.backends". Hatchling with `packages = ["src"]` works for this layout.
:::

**A8. Create src/ and the support files**

```bash title="Create src/, lock and sync"
mkdir src
touch src/__init__.py
uv lock
uv sync
```

→ `__init__.py` makes src/ a package. `uv lock` writes uv.lock, `uv sync` installs the project into .venv.

```bash title="Create the support files"
touch README.md Makefile .env.example
```

```bash title="Add placeholders to .env.example"
cat >> .env.example << 'EOF'
# Copy this file to .env and fill in your real values
# Never commit .env to Git
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here
GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-key-here
EOF
```

→ .env.example is a safe template. The real .env stays on your machine.

**A9. First commit and push**

::: warning Git Bash on Windows: paste one command at a time
Pasting multi-line blocks can create a garbage file named [200~ and commit it by accident.
:::

```bash title="Stage, check, commit, push"
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock src/ .env.example .gitignore README.md Makefile .python-version
git status
git commit -m "init: project scaffold with uv and src layout"
git push -u origin main
```

→ `git status` must list all 8 items under "Changes to be committed". After this first push, plain `git push` is enough.
### 2.3B Route B: start from GitHub with uv init

**B1. Create the repo on GitHub**

```bash title="Create repo on GitHub (web)"
# Go to github.com → click "New repository"
#
# Naming: kebab-case, all lowercase
#   my-project            ✓
#   NOT: MyProject  my_project  RAGProject
#
# Settings:
#   Repository name → my-project
#   Description     → Production RAG learning environment
#   Visibility      → Public or Private
#   ✓ Add a README file
#   ✓ .gitignore template → Python
#   ✓ License → MIT
#
# Click "Create repository"
```

→ Or create a new repository on the command line:

```bash title="Create repo on CLI"
echo "# RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD" >> README.md
git init
git add README.md
git commit -m "first commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/TheUniverseOfAI/RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD.git
git push -u origin main
```

→ Or push an existing repository from the command line:

```bash title="Push existing repo on CLI"
git remote add origin https://github.com/TheUniverseOfAI/RAG-PRODUCTION-CICD.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

**B2. Clone the repo locally**

```bash title="Clone and enter the folder"
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/my-project.git
cd my-project
```

→ Clone sets the remote origin for you. No `git remote add` needed.

**B3. Run uv init inside the cloned folder**

```bash title="Init here, pinned to Python 3.12"
uv init . --python 3.12
```

→ The dot means "init here". `uv init my-project` would create a nested subfolder.

```bash title="Delete the stub file"
rm hello.py
```

→ uv creates a placeholder script. We do not need it.

**B4. Align with the course structure**

uv init gives a base. Make it match Route A so later steps work the same.

```bash title="Add the RAG rules to .gitignore"
cat >> .gitignore << 'EOF'
.venv/
.env
.ipynb_checkpoints/
EOF
```

→ GitHub's Python template already covers most rules. These lines make sure .venv/, .env and checkpoints are ignored.

Replace the generated pyproject.toml with the one from **A7** (name `my-project`, Hatchling, ruff, pytest).

```bash title="Create src/, venv, lock and sync"
mkdir src
touch src/__init__.py
uv venv
uv lock
uv sync
touch Makefile .env.example
```

Add the .env.example placeholders from **A8**.

**B5. First commit and push**

```bash title="Commit and push"
git add .
git status
git commit -m "chore: init project with uv"
git push origin main
```

→ Your project is on GitHub from step one.

::: info Repo naming
Use kebab-case: all lowercase, words separated by hyphens. Think of the URL: github.com/you/my-project.
:::

### 2.4 Expected result and verify (both routes)

```bash title="List the project files"
find . -not -path './.venv/*' -not -path './.git/*' | sort
```

```bash title="Check Git history and remote"
git log --oneline
git remote -v
```

→ The log shows your first commit. `remote -v` shows your GitHub URL.

::: mistake Common mistakes
- **"remote origin already exists" (Route A):** run the remove-then-add pair in A4 again.
- **Push rejected, merge conflict (Route A):** the GitHub repo was created with a README or .gitignore. Route A needs an empty repo.
- **Nested folder (Route B):** you ran `uv init my-project` instead of `uv init .`.
- **"no upstream branch":** run `git push -u origin main` once.
:::

::: details Reference: complete command sequence (Route A)
```text title="Reference sequence · review before running"
# 1. Create project folder
mkdir my-project
cd my-project

# 2. Git init + connect to GitHub
git init
git branch -M main
git remote remove origin 2>/dev/null
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/my-project.git
git remote -v

# 3. .gitignore
cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
.venv/
.env
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
.DS_Store
*.egg-info/
dist/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
EOF

# 4. Pin Python + venv
uv python pin 3.12
uv venv

# 5. pyproject.toml: paste the A7 content, then
mkdir src
touch src/__init__.py
uv lock
uv sync

# 6. Support files
touch README.md Makefile .env.example

# 7. Commit and push
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock src/ .env.example .gitignore README.md Makefile .python-version
git status
git commit -m "init: project scaffold with uv and src layout"
git push -u origin main
```
:::

::: details Reference: Git essential commands
```text title="Everyday workflow"
git status                            # see what changed
git diff                              # see line-by-line changes
git add src/main.py pyproject.toml    # stage specific files
git commit -m "feat: add pdf_manager" # commit with message
git push                              # push after the first time
```

```text title="Inspecting history"
git log --oneline                     # all commits, one line each
git show HEAD                         # last commit in full
git log -p src/main.py                # history of one file
```

```text title="Undoing mistakes"
git restore --staged src/main.py      # unstage a file, keep changes
git restore src/main.py               # discard changes (destructive)
git reset --soft HEAD~1               # undo last commit, keep staged
git commit --amend -m "fix message"   # fix last commit message
```

```text title="Conventional commit prefixes"
init:   first commit, project setup
feat:   new feature or module
fix:    bug fix
deps:   package added or updated
docs:   README or documentation only
refac:  restructured code, no new behaviour
chore:  config change, cleanup
```
:::

```bash title="Verify everything is connected"
git remote -v
git log --oneline
```

→ remote -v shows your GitHub URL · log shows your first commit

```text title="Result — cloned repo with uv scaffold inside"
YOUR_REPO_NAME/
├── .git/              ← from GitHub clone
├── .gitignore         ← from GitHub (Python template)
├── README.md          ← from GitHub
├── .python-version    ← from uv init  ✓
├── pyproject.toml     ← from uv init  ✓
└── hello.py           ← delete this
```

::: info Repo naming best practices
Use kebab-case — all lowercase, words separated by hyphens. Examples: my-project, rag-learning-env, llm-notebook-hub. No underscores, no spaces, no capitals. Think about how it looks in a URL: github.com/you/my-project.
:::

::: success Why clone first, not push later?
If you run uv init my-project first then try to connect GitHub later, you have to manually set the remote origin and reconcile the README GitHub created. Clone first — uv init inside — and everything is wired automatically.
:::

::: warning GitHub .gitignore vs our RAG rules
GitHub gives you a basic Python .gitignore when you create the repo. We extend it with RAG-specific rules in Step 10 — FAISS indexes, ChromaDB SQLite, .env, and all parser outputs.
:::

::: info Commit message convention
Use conventional commits throughout the project. chore: for setup tasks, feat: for new features, fix: for bug fixes, docs: for documentation updates. Example: git commit -m "feat: add data folder structure"
:::


→ Route B also has a LICENSE file from GitHub. That is fine.

#### Details

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Project name | my-project (folder, repo and pyproject name) |
| Route A remote | Empty GitHub repo + `git remote add origin` |
| Route B remote | Set by `git clone`; `uv init .` runs inside the clone |
| pyproject.toml | Single source for metadata, dependencies and tool config |
| Build backend | Hatchling, `packages = ["src"]` |
| First commit | Route A `init: ...`, Route B `chore: ...` (conventional commits) |
